prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state

statement.case_for: Topological insulators introduced a new class of quantum matter whose protected edge and surface states follow from band topology rather than from symmetry breaking. The Kane-Mele Z2 classification is a precise, falsifiable prediction, and the HgTe quantum-well experiment confirmed it quantitatively through edge conductance. Over fifteen years the picture has held up in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and, through ARPES, in three-dimensional materials, with theory and spectroscopy agreeing. That is the combination I look for: a clear physical discovery, confirmed independently, that theory can explain, and that has reshaped how we classify and search for materials. It is a case where quantum mechanics still surprises us after a century. I also think the claim is mature, arguably overdue.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The HgTe prediction came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who are outside the credited names, and the 3D topological insulator work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and the ARPES experimentalists is also outside them. Any trio leaves out people with strong claims. Topology was also recognised in 2016, and a committee could say the field has had its prize. The technological payoff is still modest, so this prize would rest on the discovery alone.

responses.point: Goran ranks B007 sixth. He accepts that Kane and Mele supplied decisive theory and that Molenkamp's experiment was decisive. He also flags the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit, the 3D work, and overlap with the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I take the BHZ gap seriously and do not dismiss it. But BHZ predicted the effect in one material, while Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall concept that BHZ built on. Molenkamp's group then made the decisive measurement. The prize can credit the prediction of the effect together with its first observation, and the citation I propose says so. On 2016, I read it differently. Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz were honoured for topological phase transitions and topological phases in the quantum Hall and Haldane sense. Time-reversal-invariant topological insulators are a separate discovery with separate materials, and they have driven a different experimental programme.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first. She finds the idea clean and well understood, and the performance near 1e-18 confirmed independently by many laboratories. She asks whether it is precision metrology or a discovery about nature, given the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 trapped-ion prize.
responses.response: I agree with her question and think it is the main reason I rank B056 below B007. Her own framing weakens the case a little: the frequency-comb and ion-trap measurement lineage has already been recognised twice. The lattice clock is elegant and the independent confirmation is impressive. I defer to her and Stefan Kroll on the atomic physics. Still, I would want the committee to ask whether the lattice clock is a new capability built on recognised discoveries, or a new physical discovery. If the redefinition of the second goes ahead, the case becomes stronger. As a materials physicist, I see B007 as the cleaner discovery of new physics. B056 stays my first alternative.

responses.point: Stefan Kroll ranks B056 first for its measurement invention and ranks B032 third. He values aberration correction for opening up new observation in materials physics and notes the Krivanek omission.
responses.response: I appreciate the B032 argument, since aberration-corrected microscopy has changed my own field's experiments and our spectroscopy work is closely tied to it. I disagree with ranking it ahead of the topological insulators. The Krivanek omission is a real attribution problem, because the STEM corrector was an independent route. The committee would also need to decide whether this is physics or microscopy engineering. I do not hold that against it. But I think B007 has a clearer discovery of new physics at its centre. I would be happy to see B032 on a later shortlist if the attribution can be sorted out.

responses.point: Bernhard Mehlig ranks B007 first. He values Z2 invariants and protected edge states as a simple, universal organising principle. He notes that Fu, Moore, Balents and the BHZ authors have claims outside the credited names.
responses.response: I agree with the physics and share his concern about the missing theorists. Where I would go further is on the 3D case. The 3D topological insulator work was confirmed by ARPES in Bi-based materials, which is exactly the kind of spectroscopic confirmation I trust. It strengthens the maturity argument. It also shows that the credited trio is a deliberate cut through a larger field, not a complete account. I would ask the committee to settle whether the prize centres on the quantum spin Hall effect, where Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are the natural names, or on topological insulators in general, where the 3D work would need to be included.

responses.point: Mark Pearce ranks IceCube first as a new observational window with a robust, independently confirmed diffuse flux, a defensible Halzen-Karle pair and a mature field.
responses.response: I defer to Mark on astroparticle physics, and the diffuse-flux discovery looks solid to me. My reservations are those he and Ulf Danielsson raise themselves: the source identification is still at modest significance, and two names leave out many in a very large collaboration and the AMANDA lineage. I would not oppose IceCube in a later year. For this cycle I rank B007 higher because its confirmation is deeper and its attribution problem is smaller. I did not put B003 among my alternatives, only because I could not judge it well.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission, or want a configuration that credits the HgTe prediction.
Whether the 2016 prize for topological phase transitions weighs against a second topology prize, or whether the committee sees time-reversal-invariant topological insulators as a distinct discovery.
Whether Mele or another person is the right third name next to Kane and Molenkamp; the prediction credit might be allocated differently.
Whether the lattice clock should be read as a discovery or as a measurement capability, a question I leave to the atomic physics members.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My field is theoretical condensed-matter physics, and I know the topological-materials community through spectroscopy-linked electronic-structure work, but I have no apparent personal or institutional connection to Kane, Mele or Molenkamp. I have no stated connection to the other shortlisted candidates.
